newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Horn throws down gauntlet to Meciar on minorities.
newsitem.headline: Horn throws down gauntlet to Meciar on minorities.

text.p: Hungarian Prime Minister Gyula Horn challenged Slovak Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar on Friday to end delays in safeguarding the rights of Slovakia's 500,000 ethnic Hungarians.

After discussng for almost three hours with Meciar a nine-point Hungarian plan to improve relations between the two countries, Horn told a joint news conference the responsibility for ending current tensions lay squarely with the Slovak governent.

"If the plan of measures I put to Prime Minister Meciar is not implemeted it will be rather difficult to develop bilateral relations," Horn said as Meciar looked on. "And if bilateral relations do not improve the responsibility will lie with the Slovak party."

Relations between the two governments have been cool, mainly because of Slovakia's policy towards its Hungarian minority and a prolonged legal dispute over its diversion of the Danube to feed a $1 billion hydro-electric project at Gabcikovo.

Meciar and Horn signed a friendship treaty in Paris in 1995 but Hungary says Bratislava has still to implement many of its provisions, notably a law to protect the use of the mother tongue by its Hungarian minority.

Hungary is also losing patience with Slovakia's delay in setting up joint implementation committees for the treaty, mainly because it objects to ethnic Hungarian repesentatives being on the group monitoring minority rights.
Horn's memorandum to Meciar contained specific dates for setting up the committees and invited him to commit himself to passing a minorities language law by November 30.

"In these matters there has been no genuine step forward in the last three years and it is now time that the commitments undertaken by the Slovak party should finally be implemented," he said. "The situation of the Hungarians is deteriorating."
Meciar said he had agreed to the inclusion of ethnic Hungarians on the committees but left open the question whether opposition ethnic Hungarian political parties should be represented directly.
"The committee will include members of ethnic minorities who are willing to cooperate with the government," he said.

Meciar also said a bill on minority languages would be prepared but Hungary should have a similar law, a suggestion that Horn disimissed as unnecessary since language rights would be included in a general law on minorities to be passed by December.
Horn's plan also contained promises of support for Slovakia's efforts to join the European Union and NATO.
